issues.legal_issue: Whether a religious endowment deed creates an absolute dedication or only a charge in favour of the deity depends on the settlor’s intention as disclosed by the deed as a whole.
material_facts: The deed repeatedly stated that the properties were dedicated to the deity, vested absolutely in the deity, and could not be claimed by the settlor or her heirs.
The deed provided for worship and related expenses, accumulation and use of surplus income, and the succession and remuneration of shebaits, including provision for their maintenance and residence.
The deed did not reserve a beneficial interest in the properties to the settlor or her heirs; the directions benefiting shebaits and their descendants operated as charges on the endowed estate.
The evidence did not establish that the endowed property’s income substantially exceeded the specified expenses when the dedication was made.
issues.conclusion: The deed created an absolute endowment for the deity, subject to the specified charges; the properties did not remain beneficially vested in the settlor or her heirs.
issues.legal_principle: The intention to create an absolute or partial dedication is determined by a conspectus of all the deed’s provisions. If the property is wholly dedicated and no beneficial interest is reserved, the dedication is complete; if the deity receives only a charge and the residue is retained by the settlor, it is partial. Reasonable remuneration, maintenance, and residence for shebaits do not invalidate an absolute dedication. An invalid provision benefiting others does not invalidate the endowment: its benefit enures to the deity if the dedication is absolute, and to the settlor if it is partial. The Court relied on Sri Sri Iswari Bhubaneshwari Thakurani v. Brojonath Dey, L.R. 64 I.A. 203; Sree Ishwar Sridhar Jew v. Sushila Bala Dasi, [1954] S.C.R. 407; and Pande Har Narayan v. Surju Kanwari, L.R. 43 I.A. 143.

rule.if: religious_endowment_deed_case and deed_states_absolute_transfer and no_beneficial_interest_reserved and shebait_benefits_are_charges

predicates.religious_endowment_deed_case: The dispute concerns whether an instrument dedicating property for religious worship gives the deity the whole beneficial interest or only a charge.
predicates.deed_states_absolute_transfer: The settlor’s deed states that the property is dedicated to the deity and belongs to the deity absolutely.
predicates.no_beneficial_interest_reserved: The deed, read as a whole, reserves no beneficial interest in the property to the settlor, the settlor’s heirs, or another person.
predicates.shebait_benefits_are_charges: The deed provides benefits for shebaits or their descendants as charges on the endowed property rather than as a retained beneficial interest.

issues.definition: When a religious endowment deed states an absolute transfer, reserves no beneficial interest, and gives shebaits benefits only as charges, the rule treats the dedication as absolute in favour of the deity.

issues.legal_issue: Expanding income and fixed or static expenses, without more, do not establish that a religious dedication is only partial.
material_facts: The deed contained comprehensive and unrestricted terms dedicating the properties to the deity and did not reserve a beneficial interest to the settlor or her heirs.
The High Court inferred a partial dedication from the possibility that income would expand while specified expenses remained fixed.
The Supreme Court found no rule requiring that inference and held that the deed’s provisions and the settlor’s intention had to be considered as a whole.
issues.conclusion: A substantial or potentially growing surplus does not by itself require a finding of partial dedication; the settlor’s intention must be determined from the entire deed.
issues.legal_principle: Whether a dedication is absolute or partial is a question of the settlor’s intention determined by reviewing all dispositions in the deed. Surendrakeshav Roy v. Doorgasundari Dassee, L.R. 19 I.A. 108, does not establish a general presumption that expanding income and static expenses make a dedication partial; it was explained in light of its own terms and circumstances.

predicates.religious_endowment_deed_case: The dispute concerns whether an instrument dedicating property for religious worship creates an absolute dedication or only a charge.
predicates.income_may_expand: The endowed property’s income may increase over time.
predicates.specified_expenses_are_static: The deed specifies expenses that may remain fixed or fail to increase with the property’s income.

issues.definition: When a religious endowment may produce increasing income while specified expenses remain static, those circumstances alone do not establish a partial dedication.

issues.legal_issue: A joint shebait whose own rights are unaffected by a decree cannot use the appellate court’s general power to obtain relief for a non-appealing deity when the decree against the deity has become final and is severable.
material_facts: The trial court held that a dedication to deities was partial, and the deities’ court-appointed guardian did not appeal that finding.
The joint shebait appealed but did not represent the deities and did not seek a greater personal right under the deed than the trial court had awarded.
The decree concerning the deities’ interest was distinct from and could stand apart from the decree concerning the shebait’s personal rights.
The Supreme Court held that the shebait’s rights were otherwise unaffected by the decree against the deities.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the joint shebait could not invoke Order 41 rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure to obtain an absolute dedication for the non-appealing deities; the decree against them remained final.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41 rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, permits an appellate court to grant relief to a non-appealing party where necessary to adjust rights or avoid inconsistent, contradictory, or unworkable orders. It does not give an unrestricted power to reopen a final, severable decree for the benefit of a party that did not appeal when the appellant’s own rights are not affected. The majority applied this principle to the separate claims against the shebait and the deities.

predicates.appeal_from_decree_case: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree determining rights concerning a religious dedication.
predicates.deity_guardian_did_not_appeal: The guardian representing the deity did not appeal the decree made against the deity.
predicates.joint_shebait_does_not_represent_deity: The appealing joint shebait was not appointed to represent the deity in the litigation.
predicates.appellant_rights_unaffected: The decree against the deity did not affect the appealing shebait’s own rights, and the shebait did not seek greater personal rights under the instrument.
predicates.decrees_are_severable: The decree concerning the deity’s interest was distinct from the decree concerning the appellant’s personal rights and could stand independently.

issues.definition: When a deity’s guardian did not appeal, the joint shebait does not represent the deity, the appellant’s rights are unaffected, and the decrees are severable, the final decree against the deity cannot be reopened for the deity’s benefit.

issues.legal_issue: A joint shebait may appeal a decree declaring a dedication partial when that declaration affects the shebait’s own property right in the shebaitship, even if the deity’s guardian does not appeal.
material_facts: A joint shebait appealed a decree declaring that the dedication was partial rather than absolute.
The deities had independent guardians in the litigation, and those guardians did not appeal.
The dissent considered the shebaitship a property right and found that the declaration of a partial rather than absolute dedication affected the nature of that right.
issues.conclusion: In dissent, Justice Bachawat considered the appeal maintainable because the joint shebait was entitled to defend the shebaitship right affected by the decree.
issues.legal_principle: A shebait’s right is a right to property, and a decree distinguishing an absolute debutter from a partial debutter affects that right. A shebait has the right to bring proceedings necessary to protect dedicated property. The dissent relied on Maharaja Jagadindra Nath Roy Bahadur v. Rani Hemanta Kumari Debi, L.R. 31 I.A. 203; The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, [1954] S.C.R. 1005; and the authorities on the proprietary element of shebaitship cited in that opinion. This was the dissenting view; the majority held otherwise.

predicates.appeal_from_decree_case: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree determining whether a religious dedication is absolute or partial.
predicates.appellant_is_joint_shebait: The person appealing holds a joint shebaitship in respect of the deity.
predicates.decree_changes_nature_of_shebaitship_rig: The decree’s determination that the dedication is partial rather than absolute affects the appellant’s shebaitship right.

issues.definition: When a joint shebait appeals and the decree changes the nature of that shebait’s property right, the dissent would allow the shebait to appeal to defend that right.
